extracted.intended_audience: Efficiency Review (ER) teams and Department of Defense analysts conducting utilization/cost reviews of military medical treatment facilities
extracted.subtask_short: efficiency review of military medical care
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for conducting an Efficiency Review (ER) of military outpatient/inpatient medical care functions, including data sources, case-mix measurement, costing, practitioner and facility factors, and performance measurement. Focused on how an ER team should plan, collect, analyze, and assess medical care utilization and productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: ER process stages
rubrics_metrics.description: After the Medical Care area has been selected and the team assembled, the general approach is drafting the Preliminary Efficiency Review Plan; preparing the ER Performance Work Statement; conducting the ER Functional Analysis; and developing and submitting the ER Study Report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These sequential deliverables define the ER team's workflow and expected outputs during a review of a functional medical area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use all available information and expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: During development of the Preliminary ER Plan the team members will take advantage of every available source of information and expertise to become knowledgeable about the functional area to be reviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine regulations, organizational manuals, civilian literature, and conduct site visits as necessary to gain data and knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select targets by economic analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: An economic analysis is usually conducted by the ER team to identify specific activities or areas within the functional area offering the best chances for cost-containment savings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use economic prioritization to focus ER effort on activities with highest potential savings rather than attempting comprehensive review of highly complex systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine legitimate care reasons (service-requiring potential)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ER team must know why patients seek outpatient medical care to determine what is legitimate care and thus what should or should not be seen at the outpatient facility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify patient service requirements from both the patient's and the practitioner's perspectives to distinguish necessary from unnecessary utilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Donabedian's service‑requiring phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Important phenomena that indicate and can represent service-requiring potential: 1) people, 2) mortality or survival, 3) morbidity, 4) situations that require care but which cannot be classified as morbidity or mortality, and 5) health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories to frame measurement and classification of demand for services when assessing utilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess population demographics via DEERS but evaluate data quality
rubrics_metrics.description: DEERS can provide demographic data (beneficiary groups by age and sex, catchment area estimates) to support utilization and planning, but the data collected to date is not error-free and requires authentication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before relying on DEERS reports, consider these specific concerns: (1) DEERS is relatively new and error-prone; (2) validity of input remains questionable and requires careful authentication; (3) patient demographics differ markedly by location; (4) patients are free to seek civilian care without MTF permission; (5) some inpatient care under CHAMPUS occurs after MTF authorization; (6) non-catchment area patients are not required to seek MTF care; (7) active duty populations move frequently; (8) satellite outpatient demographics are included in parent MTF reports and may not be otherwise available. Many of these problems must be studied/resolved prior to using DEERS as a basis for demographic evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer case-mix adjusted output measures over crude counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional single-value measures such as outpatient visits or patient days are 'crude' and should be replaced with case-mix adjusted patient visit or patient day measures to better reflect output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust output measures for case-mix (e.g., using DRGs or similar groupings) so output reflects differences in types, intensities, durations of care and associated resource consumption rather than raw counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate suitability and limitations of DRGs for outpatient case-mix
rubrics_metrics.description: Disease Related Groupings (DRGs) provide a way to define case-mix and link case‑mix to resource-mix, producing a determinable cost-mix; they have benefits and limitations for utilization review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits listed: DRGs useful for regional utilization review, standards in prospective reimbursement, planning and budgeting, comparative efficiency measures, and patient profiles for resource scheduling. Limitations listed: statistical differences due to demographics/environment/resource-mix/policies/treatment styles; DRGs not based on actual patient costs but averages; limited variables due to data availability; patient information reliability limitations; influenced by time-changes in resources; must be updated at least yearly for consumption/time values; influenced by subjective judgments; to be valid DRGs must be regionally or locally developed to reflect patient population uniqueness. Consider these when adopting DRGs for outpatient visits—outpatient groupings for visits are less developed and pose identification/refinement challenges (intensity, duration, resource allocation).

rubrics_metrics.name: DRG-based case-mix cost methodology (Doremus approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: A stepwise approach to develop DRG-based case-mix cost data: (1) group hospitals by variables and geographic location; (2) collect demographic and clinical cost data for a sample of patients for each hospital; (3) group each patient into an appropriate DRG; (4) calculate average cost per patient per DRG; (5) calculate average cost per patient across all DRGs for hospitals in the group; (6) for each hospital, multiply proportion of hospital patients in a DRG times average DRG cost; (7) sum results for each hospital; (8) compare group average with hospital result and compute an index number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these operations to produce a hospital-specific cost index relative to group norms; requires reliable demographic, clinical, and cost data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze practitioner characteristics affecting disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner characteristics (which influence disposition decisions) include facility size, available services/resources, age, specialty, environment, health, source of education, experience, and personality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since physicians make dispositions for the majority of visits, ER analysts must measure practitioner constraints and behavioral factors to understand utilization patterns and potential areas for improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify acceptable quality standards before efficiency reforms
rubrics_metrics.description: ER process must ensure the activity being analyzed currently has acceptable quality standards and that output meets those standards (per DODI 5010.XX and other directives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for existence and adequacy of peer and utilization review standards, professional and credentialing standards, patient profile standards, facility and personnel standards, safety standards, and efforts toward inter-service consistency. Identification, implementation, and especially acceptance/utilization of standards are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine facility physical aspects, organization, staffing, and command relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: After patient and practitioner characteristics, the analyst must examine physical aspects of the facility and its relationship with its population, internal organization, staffing, and higher command structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how facility layout, separation from parent inpatient facilities, staff mix (physicians, PAs, nurse practitioners, support staff), and command constraints affect throughput, scheduling, and resource utilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costing activities and accounting limitations (Uniform Chart of Accounts)
rubrics_metrics.description: DOD directives require costing of activities being evaluated. The Uniform Chart of Accounts provides a consistent cost reporting tool for military medical departments but has limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limitations before relying on these costs: information is aggregated and not directly relatable to individual patients; costs are average unit costs allocated through layers using workload indicators; data are typically six months old; managers may question validity; there are no requirements to use the information for management control. Also, ER must consider standby/contingency capability costs, decide which perspectives to include (cost to government, cost to government and beneficiary, societal cost), include CHAMPUS/third-party/out-of-pocket costs as relevant, and examine relation between outpatient and parent inpatient facility costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data collection quality standards: accuracy, relatability, validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Information collected must be accurate, relatable and valid; local level data collection methods and responses can be sampled for utility within ER scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because local data are often deficient, ER teams should authenticate inputs, sample local collection methods, and account for data reliability when drawing conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance/productivity measurement requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Before productivity improvement decisions, performance measurement should evaluate the actual situation as part of management control systems to understand efficiency of resource allocation to planned services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures should give management knowledge about cost center efficiency, be timely, comparable, and tied to planned service quantities and acceptable quality. Establish baselines (e.g., 'How inefficient and ineffective is this function and how efficient and effective should it be?') to judge potential reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope appropriateness: apply ER to specific well-defined activities
rubrics_metrics.description: ER is intended to identify common standards of quantity and quality applicable to a functional area group and induce group-like behavior in individual elements to gain savings, but the military medical delivery system's complexity may exceed ER's practical reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize ER application to narrowly defined activities where the process can produce realistic efficiency gains; recognize that attempting ER across highly interdependent, variable, and complex medical functions may not be realistic within ER methodology, time, or cost-benefit constraints.
